documents.title: 66 Gerrard Street East - Notice of Intention to Designate a Property under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act

happening.text: The City wants to give this old building full heritage protection.
Right now it is only listed on the City's Heritage Register, a list of buildings with heritage value. It has been listed since November 6, 1974.
If it is protected, City Council could review any plan to tear it down or change it, and the City could enforce standards for looking after it.
The report doesn't mention any plan to replace this building.

why.text: A provincial law change called Bill 23 says listed buildings must either be protected or taken off the Heritage Register by January 1, 2027.
This is one of 18 old (pre-1870) listed buildings the City is looking at first. If it isn't protected by that date, it comes off the register.
It was built around 1855 as three attached brick houses, and its history is tied to Toronto's LGBTQ+ community.

where.text: At 66 Gerrard Street East (including entrance addresses at 366, 368, and 370 Church Street and 64 Gerrard Street East). This mainly matters for visitors, patrons, neighbours, and members of Toronto's LGBTQ+ community.

process.text: City staff recommended that City Council say it plans to protect the property under Ontario's heritage law.

documents.title: 2025–2026 Annual Winter Maintenance Report and Amendment to Blanket Contracts #C78, #C87, #C88 and #C89 with Rafat General Contractor Inc. for the Non-Exclusive Supply of All Labour, Equipment and Materials Necessary to Provide Single Axle, Tandem and Tri Axle Dump Trucks with Operators for Trucking Services

Families have built laneway homes whose only road access is via public lanes, and the city's current lack of snow clearing in lanes creates serious access issues for these residents during severe winter weather.

process.text: City staff recommended approving the application to amend the rules for what can be built on this site.

documents.title: Decision Report - Approval - 5, 7, 9 and 11 Bellamy Road South
Supplementary Report - 5, 7, 9 and 11 Bellamy Road South

happening.text: It is proposed to build three blocks of four-storey stacked and back-to-back townhouses with 110 homes at 5, 7, 9 and 11 Bellamy Road South.
The new townhouses would replace three detached houses.
The report doesn't mention any plan to replace this building.

why.text: The proposal aims to add family-size homes and gentle density in a stable neighbourhood close to bus service and a GO station.

where.text: At 5, 7, 9 and 11 Bellamy Road South. This mainly matters for neighbours, residents and visitors in the area.

conditions.text: At least 32% of the lot must be landscaping, with at least 50% of that being soft landscaping.
Outdoor amenity space must be provided at the rate of at least 6.0 square metres for each home.

process.text: City staff recommended approving the changes to the rules for what can be built on this site.

documents.title: 120 Donside Drive - Application for Fence Exemption

happening.text: An application was made to allow a gate fence beam at 120 Donside Drive to be 2.48 meters tall instead of the allowed 2 meters.

why.text: City rules only allow fence gates to be up to 2 meters high.
An inspection found that the horizontal beam above the east side gate is 2.48 meters high, which breaks the rules.

where.text: 120 Donside Drive, and this mainly matters for the property owner.

process.text: City staff recommended refusing to grant an exemption for the existing fence.

documents.title: Application to Remove a Private Tree – 5 Vonda Avenue

happening.text: A permit is requested to remove one silver maple tree at 5 Vonda Avenue.
If the condition of the tree worsens, the applicant can reapply for a permit to remove the tree.

why.text: The applicant wants to remove the tree due to a concern for potential future failure.
The City wants to protect healthy trees to reach its goal of 40 percent tree cover across Toronto by 2050.

where.text: At 5 Vonda Avenue, this mainly matters for the property owner and the local community.

process.text: City staff recommended that the North York Community Council deny the request for a permit to remove one privately-owned tree.

documents.title: Request for a Fence Exemption - 4 Berryton Avenue
Request for a Fence Exemption - 4 Berryton Avenue

happening.text: The property owner of 4 Berryton Avenue is asking for permission to use a Juliette-style gate and enclosure for a pool instead of building a fourth fence between the pool and the deck.
If the owner had to build a fourth fence, it would limit how people can move around that area.

why.text: The owner wants to use a Juliette-style gate at the rear access point to prevent access into the pool area.

where.text: At 4 Berryton Avenue. This mainly matters for the property owner.

process.text: City staff recommended that Etobicoke York Community Council refuse to grant the application for exemption because the fence fails to comply with the provisions of Toronto Municipal Code, Chapter 447 Fences.

documents.title: 3100 Weston Road – Zoning By-law Amendment Application – Appeal Report

happening.text: The proposal asks to build three four-storey residential buildings with 125 homes, while keeping the Carmine Stefano Community Centre and existing heritage structures on the site.
The report doesn't mention any plan to replace this building.

why.text: The applicant appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal because Council did not make a decision within the time frame set by the Planning Act.
The proposal aims to add new homes to a major street while protecting the natural environment and local heritage buildings.

where.text: At 3100 Weston Road, this mainly matters for neighbours, visitors, and people using the nearby parks, trails, and community centre.

conditions.text: A hold on building must stay in place until the owner submits a revised water, sewer and drainage report showing adequate capacity.
The owner must secure design, construction, and financial security for any new or upgraded water, sewer and drainage infrastructure needed.
The owner must submit a revised hydrological assessment report to check groundwater quality and quantity.
The owner must address all outstanding urban forestry, natural heritage, ravine protection, transportation, and urban design issues.

process.text: City staff recommended that the City Solicitor and appropriate staff attend the Ontario Land Tribunal hearing to oppose the application in its current form and continue discussions with the applicant to resolve outstanding issues.
